full_text_checked: Full text read (via Europe PMC XML): [2] eLife 2017 including figure legends, methods and peer-review/decision letter; [5] Communications Biology 2022 including methods; [6] Frontiers 2022 (main results and methods, partially). [3] J Neurosci 2019: read through the bioRxiv full-text page (first ~100k of 128k characters) via a summarizing fetch, not line by line. Abstracts only: [1] Current Biology 2013 (paywalled), [4] JEB 2019, [7] J R Soc Interface 2015 (PMC copy not open-access, publisher behind bot check), [8] and [9] 2017 Bagheri papers, [10] model paper. Not accessible: Bagheri 2017 PhD thesis PDF (host not resolvable), figshare data not downloaded. GitHub repo of [2] listed: only stimulus sequences, no analysis code.
task_and_output: Electrophysiology papers [1]-[6]: no model task; the measured output is the spike rate of a single identified neuron (CSTMD1, or small/large-field STMDs) in 100 ms windows, used to infer (a) which of two targets is selected (winner-takes-all; selection read out by frequency tagging in [3],[5]) and (b) a spatial map of gain change (primer-and-probe minus probe-alone spike rate) around the predicted target location in [2]. Model papers: [7] closed-loop simulated pursuit with an ESTMD front end plus facilitation; output is a gaze/saccade command toward the location of maximal facilitated response, scored as pursuit success; [8] open-loop tracking on video sequences, output a target location (point/box) compared with engineered trackers; [9] robot pursuit with real camera; output steering toward the selected feature. [10] dendritic-compartment model output: facilitated response magnitude. None outputs an identity decision or a calibrated 'target absent' score.
data_and_independent_videos: [2]: wild-caught male Hemicordulia (tau) dragonflies; n = 9 for the 2D focus map (Fig. 3A), n = 7 for 300 ms occlusion map (Fig. 3B) and interhemispheric map (Fig. 3C), additional n = 12 for 1D 100 vs 300 ms occlusion (Fig. 3E), n = 8 for Fig. 4E, n = 9 for contrast (Fig. 5) and direction (Fig. 6), n = 5 Fig. 7, n = 13 small-field and n = 11 large-field STMDs (Fig. 8); synthetic stimuli on a monitor, no videos. [3] (preprint numbers): 26 dragonflies, e.g. 447 trials / 13 animals for paired selection (Fig. 2), 295 trials / 7 animals priming (Fig. 5). [5]: 33 dragonflies; 389 trials / 15 animals (short primers, Fig. 1c), 507 trials / 15 (long primers), 896 trials combined (Fig. 2d), 480 trials / 13 binocular (Fig. 4b). [6]: 35 dragonflies (33 male, 2 female); 3 panoramic natural images (dense, urban, sparse) moved at 15/35/90 deg/s, two or four starting phases. Models: [7] simulated pursuits against 'heavily cluttered natural scenes' (number of scenes not verified [uncertain]); [8] public video sequences plus an own dataset of small targets embedded in natural scenes (exact datasets and counts not verified [uncertain]); [9] real-world robot runs. No train/test split concept applies: the models are hand-designed with parameters tuned to the same simulations [uncertain for [7]-[9]].
target_size_and_input_resolution: Electrophysiology: targets are 1.5 x 1.5 deg dark squares ([2], [5], [6]; 2 x 2 deg for receptive-field mapping in [5]; 1.5 x 10 deg bars as control in [3]); STMDs respond to targets smaller than about 5 deg. Drift speed 40 deg/s ([2], [3]), 50 deg/s ([5]), 25-90 deg/s ([6]). Monitor viewed at 20 cm; no explicit pixel count reported. Dragonfly eye has many thousands of ommatidia with acute-zone spacing well below 1 deg [uncertain], so a 1.5 deg target covers only a few ommatidia. Spatial scale of the effect in [2]: enhancement peak about 4 deg ahead of the last target position; a 12 deg jump gives unfacilitated response, a 20 deg jump or offsets beyond about 15 deg give surround suppression; primer region 5 deg wide. Models [7]-[9]: front end blurs images to insect-like ~1 deg acuity [uncertain]; exact input pixel resolution not verified.
frame_rate_and_camera_motion: [2]: LCD monitors at 120 Hz and above; [5]: 165 Hz; [3]: 120-165 Hz. Animal is fixed (no self-motion) in all recordings. Background: plain grey/white in [2],[3],[5]; [6] moving panoramic natural scenes (15-90 deg/s) simulating background motion, but no true ego-motion or parallax. Time scales: facilitation builds over hundreds of ms and is largely complete within ~400 ms ([5]); weaker facilitation persists >500 ms at the primed location after target disappearance ([2], Fig. 4C); cue bias diminishes over ~1000 ms ([3],[5]). Models: [7] simulated saccadic gaze; [9] real robot camera with vibration and saccades, with a feed-forward (efference-copy-like) prediction of self-motion consequences; frame rate not verified [uncertain].
detector_and_exemplar: No learned detector. Target is defined only by its spatiotemporal history: a 'primer' trajectory (or 'cue' segment preceding a pair) establishes facilitation; there is no appearance exemplar. Selection between two equally salient targets is internal (winner-takes-all) and biased by which target appeared first on a continuous path. In models [7]-[9], an ESTMD 'matched filter' (photoreceptor, LMC, rectifying transient cell, ON/OFF correlation) acts as the small-target detector; the facilitation map is centred on the previously selected target's predicted location.
trainable_nodes_and_loss: None. Electrophysiology papers have no model. [7]-[9] are hand-designed models with tuned parameters (facilitation gain, spatial extent, time constant); [7] reports that optimal facilitation parameters are 'static in space and dynamic in time' and depend on clutter and pursuit purpose, found by parameter sweeps, not gradient training [uncertain on procedure]. [10] is a biophysical compartment model with hand-set synaptic gains (NMDA-like nonlinearity). Parameter counts not given.
controls_seeds_splits: Within-animal paired controls: probe-alone vs primer-and-probe, randomly interleaved, >= 7 s rest between trials ([2]) or >= 12 s ([5]); local vs distant primer (12 deg offset) and merged model of local+distant distributions as the null for 'only the selected target is facilitated' ([5]); low vs high contrast primers ([2], Fig. 5); primers moving toward vs away from receptive field ([2], Fig. 8); background-only and grey-strip controls to remove local contrast variation ([6]); Sum/Max/Min/Switch response models compared ([6], Fig. 6). Statistics: biological replicates = animals; Cohen's d maps, paired t-tests ([2]); Wilcoxon rank-sum with Bonferroni-Holm and Hedges g with 95% CI, trials treated as independent ([5]). Exclusions: ~30% of paired trials discarded when frequency tagging could not identify the selected target ([5]); 172 of 447 trials rejected in [3] preprint. No seeds (biology). Models [7]-[9]: comparison with/without facilitation and against engineered trackers; no random-network controls; independent test sets not verified [uncertain].
metrics_and_numbers: [2] eLife 2017: focus centre spike-rate increase >50% (p = 0.0007, n = 9) and surround decrease up to 50% (p = 0.005, n = 9) (Results, Fig. 3A); Cohen's d up to +/-1.8 across maps (Fig. 3D); after a 300 ms pause the focus spreads forward (p = 0.005, n = 7; Fig. 3B); expected positions 3 deg (100 ms) and 9 deg (300 ms) ahead; forward shift 100 vs 300 ms p = 0.03, d = 0.7, n = 12 (Fig. 3E); backward jump of 6 deg resets to unfacilitated, 12 deg backward gives potent suppression (Fig. 3E); jumps 4 deg ahead = near fully facilitated, 12 deg ahead = unfacilitated, 20 deg ahead = suppressed (Fig. 4A, n = 9 technical replicates, 1 animal); occlusion-matched jumps (12 deg/300 ms, 20 deg/500 ms) increase response, d = 2.0 and 2.32, p = 0.008 each, n = 8 (Fig. 4E); at last-seen position responses decrease with pause (p = 0.0005), d = 4.48; contrast threshold 0.071 -> 0.013 and C50 0.36 -> 0.13 (>5-fold sensitivity gain, n = 9, p < 0.0001; Fig. 5C); distant primer 20 deg to the side gives no facilitation (Fig. 5C); motion after-effect hyperpolarisation ~4 mV (Fig. 5D); direction tuning shifts to the primer direction, n = 9 (Fig. 6C); reversal of trajectory gives strong long-lasting inhibition (Fig. 6F); 4 deg forward jump into focus lowers direction selectivity b1/b0 0.32 vs 0.50, p = 0.04, reversed probes facilitated only when jumped into focus (d = 3.90, Fig. 7C); facilitation >40% in small-field STMDs (p = 0.0004, n = 13), >80% in large-field STMDs (n = 11), ~50% in CSTMD1 (Fig. 8C); spontaneous rate 11 +/- 4 spikes/s. [1] CB 2013: responses to target pairs match a competitive-selection model, r^2 = 0.83 (abstract). [3] J Neurosci 2019 (preprint): selection biased toward primed trajectory (p < 0.001, Fig. 5); distracter modulation decreases with primer contrast (Kruskal-Wallis chi2 = 21.32, p < 0.001, Fig. 6B); lock-on with primer contrast as low as ~0.2 in one neuron (Fig. 6C); 71.4% of trials passed selectivity threshold; switching models fitted (Fig. 7). [5] Commun Biol 2022: local primer facilitation vs probe alone g = 2.36 [1.99, 2.72] (Fig. 1c); distant primer at 12 deg no significant effect g = 0.25 [-0.03, 0.53]; paired primers facilitated vs probe alone g = 2.36 [2.03, 2.70] and not different from local primer g = 0.19 [-0.10, 0.49], i.e. both targets of a pair are facilitated (Fig. 1c-d); local vs distant selection not different, g = 0.25 [0.006, 0.501], p = 0.052 (Fig. 2d); cue induces local selection in ~80% of trials; when the cue is ignored (~20%, 25 trials) probe response reduced vs local primer (g = 0.39), interpreted as inhibition-of-return-like suppression (Fig. 3a); in binocular pairs ~80% of uncued trials select the inhibitory-hemifield target (Fig. 4b); inhibitory-hemifield primer suppresses a subsequent excitatory probe for >= 200 ms (Fig. 5b); post-stimulus inhibition lasts >= 1 s (Fig. 5c); no difference between 400 and 800 ms primers (facilitation complete within ~400 ms; Fig. 4f). [6] Front Cell Neurosci 2022: background with target vs background+grey strip differs (p = 0.0074, n = 3, Fig. 1D); response variability to target increases with moving natural backgrounds; a 'Switch' (selection) model fits responses best among six variants (p < 0.0001, Fig. 6D); no facilitation from opposed target/background motion (Fig. 3B). [7]-[9]: facilitation 'substantially improves' pursuit success and attending to one target among distracters; tracker at least 2x faster than compared engineered trackers ([8]); feed-forward self-motion prediction 'significantly' improves detection during saccades ([9]) - exact numbers not verified [uncertain].
tested_conditions: Unseen videos: no for electrophysiology (synthetic stimuli); not reported/unclear for models [7]-[9] [uncertain]. Target absence: partially - probe-alone and background-only trials exist, and post-stimulus behaviour after target disappearance is measured ([2] Fig. 4C/E, [5] Fig. 5c), but no explicit 'target absent' decision or refusal score is evaluated. Similar distractors: yes - two identical 1.5 deg targets 12-20 deg apart ([1], [3], [5]); abrupt high-contrast distracter ([3]); natural background features as distractors ([6]); distracters in models ([7], [9]). Occlusion: yes, simulated as a pause of 100-500 ms with or without a jump ([2] Fig. 3B,E and Fig. 4C-E); not real occluders. Night or low light: no (contrast varied 0.06-1 Weber, but no low-luminance condition). Sequential operation on own predictions: no for electrophysiology (open-loop presentation, fixed animal); yes for closed-loop models [7] (simulated pursuit) and [9] (robot), where the gaze/robot follows its own selection.
mechanism_summary: Published mechanism: (1) Selection: CSTMD1 represents only one of two simultaneous targets in its spiking output (winner-takes-all, preserves the absolute response to the winner), with occasional mid-trial switches; a preceding target on the same trajectory (cue) biases which target wins, and the bias fades over ~1 s. (2) Predictive gain modulation ('facilitation'): a target moving on a continuous path creates a local focus of increased contrast and response gain (> 50% rate increase, > 5-fold contrast sensitivity) a few degrees ahead of its current position, plus broad surround suppression and strong inhibition for trajectory reversals; the focus builds over ~100-400 ms, spreads forward during a pause in proportion to the elapsed time (approximately matching constant-velocity extrapolation at 40 deg/s), weakens at the last-seen location over ~500 ms, and is nearly contrast-invariant once triggered (a 'switch' set by target presence). (3) Preattentive ordering (2022): within one hemifield, both targets of a pair generate their own focus, so facilitation precedes and gates selection rather than implementing it; switching away from a cued target leaves inhibition-of-return-like suppression; across hemifields, selection establishes ocular dominance with >= 200 ms suppression of the other side. Proposed (not published) modification for our setting: implement a recurrent, multiplicative gain field inside the FlyVis path, centred on the extrapolated previous-target position (from the last trusted track state), shifted forward with elapsed loss time, with suppressive surround and inhibition for reversed motion, and use the gated response for re-identification and refusal.
transfer_limits: 1) Scale: the effect is defined for targets of 1.5-3 deg (a few ommatidia, below ~5 deg) and a focus ~4 deg ahead with suppression beyond ~15 deg; our targets are ~9 x 12 lattice steps (hexals) inside a crop of max(2 x long side, 64 px), i.e. the target occupies a large fraction of the 721-hexal eye; STMD size tuning and the focus/surround geometry do not transfer directly and would have to be re-expressed in object-size units. 2) Frame rate: experiments used 120-165 Hz displays, but the facilitation time constants (100-400 ms build-up, ~500 ms persistence, ~1 s cue decay) correspond to ~3-30 frames at 30 Hz, so temporal scale is compatible; per-frame displacement at 30 Hz can however be large relative to the focus width for fast objects. 3) Moving and rescaling crop: the biological focus is in retinotopic world coordinates on a fixed animal; our eye is re-centred on the track prediction each frame, so the 'ahead of trajectory' location is mostly already at the crop centre; the gain field must be transformed with the crop shift/scale (equivalent to an efference copy, as in the robot [9]), otherwise it is either redundant or wrong. 4) Camera motion: recordings had no ego-motion; only [6] (moving panoramas) and [9] (robot) add background motion, and [6] shows increased variability and switching to background features. 5) Identity: the mechanism separates targets by spatiotemporal continuity, not appearance; the 2022 result that BOTH similar targets on consistent paths get facilitated means it cannot by itself pick the previous target among similar neighbours whose motion is also consistent - exactly our failure mode. It adds little beyond the Kalman/IoU gating ByteTrack already does. 6) Refusal: there is no published calibrated absence signal; a decaying focus after disappearance could serve as a prior for 'too long lost -> refuse', but no evidence links it to localisation quality. 7) Environment: YOLO26s already detects objects; the mechanism's strength (detecting tiny low-contrast targets in clutter) is not our bottleneck. 8) FlyVis has no lobula/STMD layer; implementing facilitation 'inside' FlyVis requires adding a recurrent gain state on existing cell types (e.g. multiplicative gain on input or on T4/T5/Tm output activity), which is a new node, not a reuse of a trained one.
research_questions_addressed: Q1 (direct evidence, but caution): the strongest insect evidence for choosing ONE of two similar targets; selection is by trajectory history and onset order, not by exemplar appearance; refusal is not studied. Answer for Q1 per outline: the mechanism exists in insect neurophysiology with quantitative but simple-stimulus evidence (synthetic squares, fixed animal, no moving camera except robot) -> low direct transferability. Q3 (direct evidence on operating range): small targets 1.5-3 deg, 120-165 Hz display, fixed animal; time constants compatible with 30 Hz, spatial scale not compatible with ~9 x 12-hexal targets. Q2 (design analogy): suggests that a state/dynamics node (persistent spatial gain) is a distinct change from readout changes; gives no procedure to separate representation from readout. Q4 (caution): the facilitation 'switch' is nearly contrast-invariant and drives responses to saturation to reduce variability - the opposite of a calibrated confidence; IoR-like suppression after switching is a design idea for avoiding returning to a rejected neighbour. Q5 (design analogy): a gain field is cheap (few parameters, no training needed) and can be tested on cached loss episodes with three-way control.
candidate_node_change: Node: dynamics/state transfer - a 'predictive gain field' state inside the FlyVis path. Each frame during loss, form a 2D gain map on the hexal lattice: multiplicative enhancement (Gaussian, width ~ one object half-size, gain g) centred on the extrapolated previous-target position mapped into the current crop coordinates (crop shift and scale applied as an efference-copy transform), shifted forward by v * t_lost, broad surround suppression (width ~ 2-3 object sizes), and an inhibition-of-return term at positions of neighbours already rejected. Apply it as a gain on FlyVis input photoreceptor drive or on selected output cell types (T4/T5, Tm) before the object readout; carry the field as recurrent state with decay time ~0.3-0.5 s (10-15 frames at 30 Hz), reset on confident re-acquisition. Controls (rule 6.16): (1) stand without change; (2) same gain field applied without FlyVis - on the crop pixels/feature map of network B (~9602 params) or simply as a Kalman-distance prior on candidate scores; (3) the same field with stock frozen FlyVis (C) and with the trained core (D). Minimal check (cheap, cached data): on existing loss episodes with similar neighbours, measure top-1 correct re-identification among candidates and the useful-correction rate at fixed coverage, versus a pure nearest-to-prediction baseline; then one MASA-HOTA run only if (3) beats (2). Stop condition: stop if (3) minus (2) paired-bootstrap CI over videos includes 0 for the re-identification metric, or if (2) alone equals or beats (3) (then it is a tracker-gating improvement, not a FlyVis result), or if gain field does not beat the nearest-to-prediction baseline by a pre-registered margin (e.g. +2 p.p. useful centres) [uncertain margin, to be set by author].
strongest_objection: The published mechanism is a spatiotemporal continuity prior - essentially a biologically implemented constant-velocity predictor with gating - and the 2022 preattentive result shows it facilitates every target on a consistent path, so it does not discriminate the previous target from similar neighbours moving coherently; our tracker already has this prior (Kalman prediction, crop centred on prediction), so the expected added value for re-finding among similar neighbours is small and, if any, would likely appear equally in the no-FlyVis control. Moreover, the evidence comes from a fixed animal viewing 1.5 deg synthetic squares at 120-165 Hz, with no ego-motion and no large or textured targets; the model/robot papers whose settings are closer (video, camera motion) could not be verified in full text and report no public code.
evidence_strength: Electrophysiology [1]-[3], [5], [6]: peer-reviewed, consistent within one lab (Adelaide/Lund), repeated across several papers and animals (n = 7-33 dragonflies), large effect sizes; no independent replication by another lab found; stimulus scripts and figshare data for [2] available, no analysis code. Strength: strong for the existence of selection and predictive facilitation in CSTMD1; weak for transfer to our task. Models [7]-[9]: peer-reviewed, same lab, no public code found, full text not verified here -> weak to moderate. Overall for our decision: weak (design analogy only).
